extracted.intended_audience: federal trial judges, jurors, and patent litigators in U.S. patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for determining patent infringement and validity in U.S. federal trials. Covers doctrine of equivalents, means-plus-function claim rules, contributory and induced infringement, willfulness, and validity standards (anticipation, obviousness, written description, enablement, best mode, statutory bars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents — role of interchangeability and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Known interchangeability may support a conclusion that the difference between the [part] [step] in the [product] [method] and the claim requirement is not substantial. The fact that a [part] [step] of the [product] [method] performs the same function as the claim requirement is not, by itself, sufficient to show known interchangeability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Known interchangeability is supportive but not required to find infringement under the doctrine of equivalents; mere performance of the same function alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents — limitation by prior art/obviousness/prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not use the doctrine of equivalents to find infringement if you find that [alleged infringer]’s [product] [method] is the same as what was in the prior art before the application for the [ ] patent or what would have been obvious to persons of ordinary skill in the field in light of what was in the prior art. A patent holder may not obtain, under the doctrine of equivalents, protection that it could not have lawfully obtained from the Patent and Trademark Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accused product is shown to be in the prior art, burden shifts to patent holder to prove what it attempts to cover under DOE is not in the prior art or would not have been obvious. Prosecution history estoppel and prior art can bar DOE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents — limitation by subject matter described but not claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not use the doctrine of equivalents to find infringement if you find that the subject matter alleged to be equivalent to a requirement of the patent claim was described in the [ ] patent but not covered by any of its claims. The subject matter described but not claimed must be specific enough that one of ordinary skill in the art would understand that it was present in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material described in the specification but intentionally not claimed can prevent DOE coverage of that material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims — literal scope (§112(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A means-plus-function requirement only covers the specific [structure] disclosed in a patent specification for performing the claimed function and the equivalents of those specific [structure] that perform the claimed function. A means-plus-function requirement does not cover all possible structures that could be used to perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'means for processing data' is interpreted to cover the actual means disclosed in the patent for processing data and other means equivalent to it, not every possible means (e.g., pencil-and-paper or human brain) unless so disclosed or equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims — literal infringement proof steps
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide if [patent holder] has proven that [alleged infringer]’s [product] includes structure covered by a means-plus-function requirement, first decide whether the [product] has any structure that performs the described function. If not, the claim is not infringed. If it does, determine whether that structure is the same as or equivalent to the structure identified in the specification; if same or equivalent, the means-plus-function requirement is satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court (judge) may identify the corresponding structure in the specification. Equivalence requires showing a person of ordinary skill would consider differences not substantial and that the structure was available on the patent grant date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims — temporal limitation on equivalents (§112(6) vs DOE)
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalent structure under §112(6) cannot embrace technology developed after the issuance of the patent because the literal meaning of a claim is fixed upon its issuance. Although an after-arising equivalent may infringe under the doctrine of equivalents, it generally cannot infringe literally under §112(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under §112(6) the accused device must perform the identical function as recited in the claim element; DOE can be satisfied when the function is only substantially the same. The §112(6) equivalent must have been available as of the patent issuance date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (method) — step-plus-function adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim at issue is a method claim with a limitation written in 'step-plus-function' format, substitute 'acts' for 'structure' and apply the corresponding means-plus-function rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify instruction wording for method claims accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function under Doctrine of Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A means-plus-function requirement can be met under the doctrine of equivalents if the function is not the same but is equivalent, or if the corresponding structure in the accused product is later-developed technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single model instruction provided — analysis is case specific; consider Federal Circuit precedents (e.g., WMS Gaming, Chiuminatta, Al-Site).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Doctrine of Equivalents due to claim amendments/statements (prosecution history estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because [patent holder] made certain claim changes or statements during the patent application process for the [ ] patent, the doctrine of equivalents analysis cannot be applied to the following requirements of the asserted claims: [List requirements on a claim-by-claim basis]. Unless each of these requirements is literally present within the [alleged infringer]’s [product] [method], there can be no infringement of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution history estoppel or related prosecution statements can carve out subject matter from DOE coverage; judge should identify the affected claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement — elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement exists if: (1) someone other than [alleged infringer] directly infringed a claim of the [ ] patent; and (2) [alleged infringer] supplied an important component of the infringing part of the [product] or [method]; (3) the component is not a common component suitable for non-infringing use; and (4) [alleged infringer] supplied the component with knowledge of the [ ] patent and knowledge that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no direct infringement by anyone, there can be no contributory infringement. The supplier must know of the patent and that the component was specially made/adapted for infringing use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'common component suitable for non-infringing use'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'common component suitable for non-infringing use' is a component that has uses other than as a component of the patented product or other than in the patented method, and those other uses are not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the component has substantial, non-infringing uses, contributory infringement is precluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducing infringement — elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be liable for inducement of infringement, [alleged infringer] must: (1) have intentionally taken action that actually induced direct infringement; (2) have been aware of the [ ] patent; (3) have known that the acts it was causing would infringe the patent; and (4) not have had a good faith belief the patent was invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these four requirements are not met, liability may still attach if the actor believed it was highly probable its actions would cause infringement of a patent it believed valid and deliberately avoided learning the truth. Mere indifference or taking a substantial, unjustified risk is insufficient. Consider whether alleged inducer relied on advice of counsel or actually believed noninfringement/invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — standard (subjective and objective prongs)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove willful infringement, [patent holder] must first persuade you that the [alleged infringer] infringed a valid [and enforceable] claim. In addition, [patent holder] must persuade you that it is highly probable that [alleged infringer] acted with reckless disregard of the claims of the [patent holder]’s [patent].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reckless disregard requires persuasion that alleged infringer actually knew, or it was so obvious that it should have known, that its actions constituted infringement. Consider all facts surrounding the alleged infringement, including industry standards and reliance on opinion of counsel (if invoked). The judge ultimately decides the objective legal question of whether a reasonable person would have thought there was a high likelihood of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness — factors tending to show non-willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that may be considered as evidence that [alleged infringer] was not willful include: (1) whether [alleged infringer] acted in a manner consistent with the standards of commerce for its industry; and (2) whether [alleged infringer] relied on a legal opinion that was well-supported and believable advising noninfringement or invalidity (if relied upon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no affirmative obligation to obtain an opinion of counsel; include bracketed language only if alleged infringer relies on advice of counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness — factor tending to show willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that may be considered as showing willfulness includes whether [alleged infringer] intentionally copied a product of [patent holder] covered by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional copying is a strong indicator of willful conduct but must be evaluated in the full context of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove invalidity of any patent claim, [alleged infringer] must persuade you that it is highly probable that the claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the alleged infringer submits prior art not considered by the PTO during prosecution, you may take into account that such prior art may carry more weight than art that was considered by the PTO and may make the alleged infringer’s burden easier to sustain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the patent does not contain an adequate written description of the claimed invention. The purpose is to demonstrate that the inventor was in possession of the invention at the time the application was filed. The requirement is satisfied if a person of ordinary skill reading the original application at filing would have recognized that the application described the invention as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description need not use the exact words of the claim; a claim requirement may be satisfied if it is necessarily implied in the original application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the patent at the time it was originally filed did not contain a description sufficiently full and clear to enable a person of ordinary skill in the field to make and use the full scope of the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining whether excessive experimentation is required, consider: scope of the claimed invention; amount of guidance in the patent; amount, time and cost of necessary experimentation; how routine experimentation is in the field; whether patent discloses specific working examples; nature and predictability of the field; and level of ordinary skill. Enablement is judged as of the original filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the patent does not disclose what the inventor believed was the best way to carry out the claimed invention at the time the patent application was filed. The disclosure must be detailed enough to enable persons of ordinary skill to carry out that best mode without excessive experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on inventor's subjective belief at filing. Applies only to civil actions commenced prior to September 16, 2011 (AIA changed enforcement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) — all-elements-in-single-reference test
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention is not new. For anticipation, all of its requirements must have existed in a single device or method or been described in a single previous publication or patent that predates the claimed invention. The description need not use the same words, but all claim requirements must be present either stated or necessarily implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ways to show anticipation include prior public knowledge/use, prior printed publication or patent anywhere in the world, prior making by someone else, prior issued/published U.S. patent/application, learning the invention from another, or first-inventor disputes (conception and reduction to practice rules). Tailor the applicable list to the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bars (one-year bars)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the patent application was not filed within the time required by law (statutory bar). For a statutory bar, all claimed requirements must have been present in one prior art reference dated more than one year before the patent application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: printed publication more than one year before filing; public use in the U.S. not primarily experimental; sale or offer for sale in the U.S. more than one year before filing (unless primarily experimental); foreign patent obtained more than one year before U.S. filing. Disclosure need not use exact words but must enable one of ordinary skill to make and use the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Graham factors and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the time of the application. The determination requires factual findings on: (1) the level of ordinary skill in the field; (2) the scope and content of the prior art; and (3) the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art. Additionally, determine whether any of the following have been established: commercial success, long-felt need, unsuccessful attempts by others, copying, unexpected and superior results, acceptance by others, independent invention, and other evidence tending to show nonobviousness or obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court makes the ultimate legal determination of obviousness based on underlying factual determinations (often made by the jury). Present only the disputed Graham factors to the jury as necessary; secondary considerations (aka objective indicia) should be considered when supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role division between jury and judge on obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The court is charged with making the determination as to whether a patent claim was obvious based upon your determination of several factual questions. The ultimate judgment of obviousness is a legal determination for the judge, while the jury may be asked to determine underlying factual issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury should be presented with the specific factual issues in dispute (Graham factors); the judge then applies the law to those facts to reach the legal conclusion.
